title: Hidden and Revealed Members: The Body as Likeness of the Father, the Luminaries, and the Revealing Tongue
arc: From the observation that the body has both hidden inner members and revealed outer members, the teaching builds a sustained correspondence: the Father dwells hidden in his Greatness while the two ships of light and the proclaiming tongue (Jesus the Radiance) are his revealed members, sent forth to manifest every matter, including the wound of the Living Soul and her healing.
reading:
This teaching takes the structure of the human body as a single extended likeness of the divine order, and works the comparison through three parallel registers: the Father in his Greatness, the two luminaries in the cosmos, and the tongue that speaks from within the body. The argument depends on a simple observation about the body of flesh: some of its members are hidden inside and never come forth into the open, while others are set outwardly and are touched, seen, and "receive honor in fullness." Some interior members are not touched at all and do not receive that outward honor; they remain in their hidden state. This double structure — hidden interior and manifest exterior — is the natural figure that the entire teaching uses to read the divine order.

First applied to the highest register, the figure says that the entire Greatness is like the body in this respect. Within the Greatness, one is hidden and one is revealed forth; one stands far from the honor of the Height (in interior reserve) while another is touched and receives that honor in fullness. Just as the teaching of the body — that is, the inner doctrine of bodily life — is set within the storehouses of the body and not manifested forth, so the Father, the God of Truth, abides hidden in his kingship and is not manifested before "this place of emptiness which is outside," that is, the cosmos in its mingled state. The Father in his inmost Divine is the supreme hidden member; he does not come out into the outer space of the world directly. What appears outwardly is something else — his revealed members.

The teaching then names those revealed members at two levels. In the cosmos, they are the two eyes of the body, which are unhidden, manifest, and give light to the whole body: these correspond to the two ships of light, the Radiances (sun and moon) which are manifested forth in the whole world and the whole creation, and whose light has never been hidden. Like the two eyes, they are visible members through which the unseen interior shines outward. The soul, while she lives, is likened to one who stands fast in stillness and is herself manifested through such openings; but in this same stillness she is touched by the parts of the flesh that destroy her, and so she "receives honor" mingled with wound and plague — the suffering of the Living Soul in the body, dispersed in the natural and pierced by what grasps her.

The second revealed member is the tongue. The tongue, set in the body, is what speaks, proclaims, reproves, and reveals forth concerning every matter that exists in the body — both the glory and the shame of the body, the pain, the sickness, the stripe. The tongue is the body's own faculty of revelation: it brings what is hidden inside out into expression. By this likeness Jesus the Radiance is now identified. He is the one whom they send forth from the Greatness to reveal and manifest forth concerning every matter — outside and within, upper and lower, the hidden aeons that are not manifest as well as the ships of Light that are manifest. He is the revealing tongue of the Father. Through him the glory and the Greatness that dwells within the hidden aeons are spoken outwardly; through him also the wound and plague of the Living Soul — her suffering in the flesh — are proclaimed, and so too her purification and her healing.

The whole arc therefore moves from the bodily observation to a christological conclusion. The Father is hidden as the inmost members are hidden; the luminaries are revealed as the eyes are revealed; and Jesus the Radiance is revealed as the tongue is revealed — the sent member who brings the inmost Greatness into outward proclamation, whose specific work is to declare both the captivity of the Living Soul and the way of her cleansing. What at first looks like a static anatomical comparison is in fact a teaching about the structure of revelation itself: the Father remains hidden in his kingship, and what appears in the cosmos appears precisely as the manifesting members of that hidden Divine — light to be seen, and a voice to make the soul's wound, and her healing, known.
